note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/09 The Periodic Table: chemical periodicity/9.1 Periodicity of physical properties of the elements in Period 3.md
outline: Across Period 3, increasing nuclear charge shrinks atoms. Ionic radii decrease within each isoelectronic cation or anion series, with a jump between them. Melting points depend on the structures: metallic Na–Al, giant covalent Si, then simple molecular P₄, S₈ and Cl₂, and monatomic Ar. Mobile delocalised electrons make the metals good electrical conductors; Si is a semiconductor and the remaining elements do not conduct.

misconceptions.statement: Atomic radius increases across Period 3 because more electrons are added.
misconceptions.refutation: Electrons enter the same main shell while nuclear charge rises; attraction increases and atomic radius decreases.
misconceptions.contrast: More shells increase radius down a group, not across this period.

misconceptions.statement: The radii of the common ions decrease smoothly across the whole period.
misconceptions.refutation: Cation radii decrease from Na⁺ to Al³⁺, then there is a jump to the much larger anions; anion radii decrease from P³⁻ to Cl⁻.

misconceptions.statement: Silicon melts by overcoming intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.refutation: Silicon is a giant covalent lattice; melting requires breaking strong covalent bonds.
misconceptions.contrast: Instantaneous dipole–induced dipole attractions between S₈ molecules are overcome when sulfur melts.

misconceptions.statement: Silicon conducts as well as a metal because it has four outer electrons.
misconceptions.refutation: Silicon is a semiconductor; it lacks the abundant freely moving delocalised electrons of metals.
misconceptions.contrast: Na, Mg and Al are metallic conductors.

worked.problem: Explain why silicon melts at a much higher temperature than sulfur.

steps.do: Identify silicon as a giant covalent lattice and sulfur as simple S₈ molecules.
steps.why: The kind of structure determines which attractions melting must overcome.

steps.do: State that melting silicon breaks many strong Si–Si covalent bonds.
steps.why: There are no separate silicon molecules in this lattice.

steps.do: State that melting sulfur overcomes weaker instantaneous dipole–induced dipole attractions between S₈ molecules.
steps.why: The S–S covalent bonds inside each molecule remain intact.

faded.problem: Silicon melts at a much higher temperature than phosphorus. Which explanation correctly identifies the structures and attractions overcome? Enter 1, 2 or 3. (1) Silicon has a giant covalent lattice and melting breaks strong Si–Si covalent bonds; phosphorus consists of P₄ molecules and melting overcomes weaker instantaneous dipole–induced dipole attractions between molecules, leaving P–P bonds intact. (2) Both elements consist of simple molecules, but silicon has stronger intermolecular attractions. (3) Melting phosphorus breaks P–P covalent bonds, while melting silicon only overcomes intermolecular attractions.

items.stem:
Elements D and E are both in Period 3. Element D has the smallest atomic radius in Period 3.
There are only two elements in Period 3 which have a lower melting point than element E.
Elements D and E react together to form compound L.
Which compound could be L?

options.A: MgCl ₂
options.B: MgS
options.C: Na₂S

items.explanation: Chlorine has the smallest atomic radius and phosphorus has the third-lowest melting point (only argon and chlorine are lower). Thus PCl₃ fits. MgCl₂ is wrong because magnesium is too high melting.

first ionisation energy and the lowest melting point of these three elements.
What are the identities of X, Y and Z?
X

options.A: Na Mg Al
options.B: Mg Al Si

items.explanation: Phosphorus lies between silicon and sulfur. Its simple molecular structure gives the lowest melting point of the three, while its first ionisation energy exceeds sulfur’s owing to the half-filled 3p subshell.

items.stem:
Which statements are correct going across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine?
1
The charge on the nucleus increases, pulling the electrons closer to it.
2
The radius of the most common ion of each element decreases.
3
The shielding caused by inner electrons decreases, so the outer electrons are pulled closer
to the nucleus.

options.A: A
options.B: B
options.C: C

items.explanation: Nuclear charge increases and outer electrons occupy the same main shell, so atomic radius falls. Common ionic radii do not decrease smoothly because of the jump from small cations to larger anions; inner-shell shielding does not decrease.

items.stem:
Which statements help to explain the increase in melting point from sodium to aluminium?
1
The charge on the metal ion increases.
2
There are more delocalised electrons per metal ion.
3
The radius of the metal ion decreases.

options.A: A
options.B: B
options.C: C

items.explanation: All three stated changes strengthen metallic bonding: greater cation charge, more delocalised electrons and smaller ions. A first-ionisation-energy trend alone does not explain the melting points.

Which factor explains the increase in melting points from sodium to aluminium?

options.A: the change in first ionisation energy from sodium to aluminium
options.B: the increase in electronegativity from sodium to aluminium
options.C: the increase in the Ar of the elements from sodium to aluminium
options.D: the increase in the number of outer electrons in each atom from sodium to aluminium

items.explanation: More outer electrons contribute to the delocalised sea from Na to Al, strengthening metallic bonding. Increasing relative atomic mass does not explain this rise.

items.stem: Which row gives the best description of the variations in the melting points and the first ionisation energies of the elements in Period 3 from sodium to argon?

options.A: Melting points: increase up to a peak at aluminium then decrease; first ionisation energies: generally decrease.
options.B: Melting points: increase up to a peak at aluminium then decrease; first ionisation energies: generally increase.
options.C: Melting points: increase up to a peak at silicon then decrease; first ionisation energies: generally decrease.
options.D: Melting points: increase up to a peak at silicon then decrease; first ionisation energies: generally increase.

items.explanation: D is the best overall description: first ionisation energies generally increase across Period 3, with dips at aluminium and sulfur. Melting point reaches its maximum at silicon, not aluminium; the subsequent overall decrease includes a rise from phosphorus to sulfur, so it is not monotonic.

items.stem:
X and Y are atoms of different elements in Period 3 of the Periodic Table. Neither X nor Y is argon.
X is a non-metal.
X has a greater atomic radius than Y.
Which statement is correct?

options.A: X has more occupied electron shells than Y.
options.B: X has more protons in each atom than Y.
options.C: X has the same number of outer electrons in each atom as Y.

items.explanation: Atomic radius decreases across Period 3. A non-metal X with larger radius than Y must lie before Y, so Y is also a non-metal; X cannot have more protons.

items.stem: Which row about silicon, Si, and magnesium, Mg, and their ions is correct?

options.A: Si has a greater atomic radius than Mg. Explanation: Si has electrons in 3p orbitals. Mg has electrons in the 3s orbital only.
options.B: Si has a lower electrical conductivity than Mg. Explanation: Si has 4 delocalised electrons per atom. Mg only has 2 delocalised electrons per atom.
options.C: Si has a lower melting point than Mg. Explanation: Si has covalent bonding. Mg has metallic bonding.
options.D: The radius of Si⁴⁺ is smaller than the radius of Mg²⁺. Explanation: Si has a greater nuclear charge than Mg.

items.explanation: D is correct: Si⁴⁺ and Mg²⁺ each have 10 electrons, but silicon has 14 protons and magnesium has 12, so the greater nuclear attraction makes Si⁴⁺ smaller. A has the atomic-radius trend reversed. B gives a true conductivity comparison but a false explanation: silicon does not have four delocalised electrons per atom. C has the melting-point comparison reversed; silicon melts at a higher temperature than magnesium.

items.stem: Which statement is correct?

options.A: The atomic radius of silicon is larger than that of aluminium.
options.B: The boiling point of chlorine is higher than that of silicon.
options.C: The first ionisation energy of sulfur is greater than that of phosphorus.
options.D: The electrical conductivity of magnesium is greater than that of sodium.

items.explanation: Magnesium conducts better than sodium because it supplies more delocalised electrons and has stronger metallic bonding. Silicon is smaller, not larger, than aluminium.

items.stem:
X and Y are two elements from Period 3 of the Periodic Table.
Element X has a higher electrical conductivity than element Y. Element Y has a higher melting
point than element X.
Which formula is a compound formed from element X and element Y?

options.A: MgS
options.B: Mg₂Si
options.C: NaCl

items.explanation: Magnesium conducts better than silicon, but silicon melts at a higher temperature; Mg₂Si is the corresponding compound. NaCl fails the melting-point ordering.

items.stem:
Elements Y and Z are both in Period 3. Element Y has the smallest atomic radius in Period 3.
There are only two elements in Period 3 that have a lower melting point than element Z.
Elements Y and Z react together to form compound R.
Which compound could be R?

options.A: MgCl ₂
options.B: MgS
options.C: Na₂S

items.explanation: Y is chlorine; Z is phosphorus, whose melting point is exceeded below only by chlorine and argon. They form PCl₃. Magnesium has a much higher melting point.

items.stem:
Which set of three elements contains a single element that has both the highest melting point
and the lowest electrical conductivity of the three elements in the set?

options.A: magnesium, aluminium and silicon
options.B: aluminium, silicon and phosphorus
options.C: sodium, magnesium and aluminium

items.explanation: Silicon has the highest melting point and lowest conductivity among Mg, Al and Si. In the aluminium–silicon–phosphorus set, phosphorus conducts least but silicon melts highest.

items.stem: Describe the change in atomic radius from sodium to chlorine.

options.A: It decreases as nuclear charge increases within the same occupied main shell.
options.B: It increases because an electron is added at each step.
options.C: It remains constant because the shell number stays three.
options.D: It decreases because inner-shell shielding vanishes.

items.explanation: It decreases as nuclear charge increases within the same occupied main shell. The tempting alternative in B is wrong: It increases because an electron is added at each step.

options.D: Neither conducts because both are solids.

items.stem: Which statement explains why calcium has a higher melting point than barium?

options.A: Calcium cations are smaller than barium cations and have a stronger attraction to the delocalised electrons.
options.B: The structure of calcium is partly giant molecular.
options.C: There are more delocalised electrons in calcium than in barium as it has a lower ionisation energy.
options.D: There is greater repulsion between barium atoms as they have more complete electron shells than calcium atoms.

items.explanation: A is correct. This applies the metallic-bonding model used for Period 3 to two Group 2 metals: both supply two delocalised electrons per atom, but the smaller calcium cations attract the delocalised electrons more strongly. Both metals have metallic structures; additional electron shells do not explain the trend by increased repulsion.

X, Y and Z are elements all found within Groups 13, 14 and 15 of the Periodic Table.
X is in the same group in the Periodic Table as Y.
Y and Z are in Period 3.
The first ionisation energy of X is greater than the first ionisation energy of Y.
The melting point of Z is less than the melting point of Y.
Y and Z both form chlorides which are white solids. These white solids react with water to produce solutions with a pH of less than 4.
Which row of the table shows the possible identities of X and Y?

options.A: X = B; Y = Al
options.B: X = Ge; Y = Si
options.C: X = As; Y = P

items.explanation: A is correct, with X = boron, Y = aluminium and Z = phosphorus. The chloride clues are consistent with solid AlCl₃ and PCl₅. X must be above Y in its group to have the higher first ionisation energy, eliminating B and C. D is tempting, but if Y were phosphorus, neither aluminium nor silicon could be Z because both melt at higher temperatures than phosphorus; the required lower melting point is impossible.
items.examiner: The most commonly chosen incorrect answer was D. Since X and Y are in the same group of the Periodic Table, and the first ionisation energy of X is greater than the first ionisation energy of Y, X is above Y in its group. The answer therefore cannot be B or C. If the answer is D and Y is phosphorus, Z would have to be aluminium or silicon, but neither element has a lower melting point than phosphorus. If X = boron, Y = aluminium and Z = phosphorus all the information in the question is correct, so the answer is A.

flashcards.front: Describe the atomic-radius trend across Period 3.
flashcards.back: Atomic radius decreases from sodium to chlorine because nuclear charge increases while shielding by inner shells is approximately constant.

flashcards.front: Describe the common ionic-radius trend across Period 3.
flashcards.back: Cation radii decrease from Na⁺ to Al³⁺; there is a jump to larger anions; anion radii decrease from P³⁻ to Cl⁻.

flashcards.front: Describe the melting-point and conductivity patterns across Period 3.
flashcards.back: Melting point rises from Na to Si, drops at P, rises at S, then drops to Cl and Ar. Na, Mg and Al conduct well; Si is a semiconductor; P, S, Cl and Ar do not conduct.

9701-9.1.1.motivate: A Period 3 graph has several bends and one striking jump. Understanding where each appears lets you recognise an element from a physical-property clue.
9701-9.1.1.establish: Across Period 3, atomic radius decreases as nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same main shell and inner-shell shielding stays approximately constant. Common ionic radii decrease from Na⁺ to Al³⁺, jump to the larger anions, then decrease from P³⁻ to Cl⁻; each of those groups is isoelectronic. Melting point rises from Na through Mg and Al to a maximum at Si, falls sharply at P, rises at S, then falls at Cl and Ar. Na, Mg and Al conduct electricity well; Si is a semiconductor; P, S, Cl and Ar do not conduct. The repeating variation in properties across a period is periodicity.
9701-9.1.1.connect: The radius argument extends your earlier work on nuclear charge and shielding. The irregular melting-point and conductivity patterns become meaningful once you classify each element's structure.
9701-9.1.1.note:
- Atomic radius decreases across Period 3 as nuclear attraction rises.
- Common cation radii decrease; a jump separates them from the larger anions, whose radii then decrease.
- Melting point peaks at Si, drops at P, rises at S, then falls to Ar.
- Na, Mg and Al conduct well; Si is a semiconductor; P, S, Cl and Ar do not conduct.
9701-9.1.1.self_explain: Why can you describe the ionic radii as two decreasing series but not as one smooth decrease across the period?

discover.stem: Which change occurs from Na⁺ to Al³⁺?

options.A: Ionic radius decreases.
options.B: Ionic radius increases.
options.C: A new occupied shell is added.

discover.explanation: These ions have the same electron configuration, but nuclear charge rises.

9701-9.1.2.motivate: Silicon melts far above sulfur but conducts far worse than aluminium. Structure and bonding explain both comparisons.
9701-9.1.2.establish: Na, Mg and Al have metallic lattices. From Na to Al, smaller ions with greater charge attract more delocalised electrons more strongly, so melting points rise; mobile delocalised electrons carry current. Si has a giant covalent lattice: many strong Si–Si bonds must break on melting, giving the period's highest melting point. Si is a semiconductor, not a good metal-like conductor. P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ are simple molecules, and Ar is monatomic. Melting overcomes weak instantaneous dipole–induced dipole attractions between their particles; it does not break the covalent bonds inside molecules. S₈ has stronger attractions than P₄ because it is larger and has more electrons. These non-metals lack mobile charged particles, so they do not conduct.
9701-9.1.2.connect: Use the structure categories from bonding: metallic, giant covalent, simple molecular and monatomic. For every property, name the particles that move or the attraction that melting overcomes.
9701-9.1.2.note:
- Na–Al: stronger metallic bonding raises melting points; mobile delocalised electrons conduct.
- Si: giant covalent lattice, high melting point, semiconductor.
- P₄, S₈, Cl₂ and Ar: weak attractions between particles give lower melting points.
- P, S, Cl and Ar have no mobile charged particles and do not conduct.
9701-9.1.2.self_explain: What is broken when sulfur melts, and how does that differ from what is broken when silicon melts?

discover.stem: Why is silicon's melting point much higher than sulfur's?

options.A: Si–Si covalent bonds in a giant lattice are much stronger than attractions between S₈ molecules.
options.B: Silicon molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.
options.C: Sulfur has weak covalent bonds within S₈ that break on melting.
options.D: Silicon has more delocalised electrons than sulfur.

discover.explanation: Silicon is giant covalent; sulfur is simple molecular, so different attractions are overcome on melting.
